Subtract 3 from both sides: 5x = 49, so x = 49/5. A linear equation with a nonzero coefficient on x has exactly one solution. It would have zero or infinitely many solutions only if the x-terms cancelled out.

Since (−6, 0) is on the graph, h(−6) = 0. The factors x − 4 and 2x − 6 aren't zero at x = −6, so x + p must be: −6 + p = 0, giving p = 6. Then h(0) = (0 + 6)(0 − 4)(0 − 6) = 6(−4)(−6) = 144. Note that h(0) is just the product of the three constant terms.

Adding 18 gives ax ≤ 32. The solution set x ≥ −8 points the opposite way, so dividing by a must have flipped the inequality, which means a is negative: x ≥ 32/a. Matching gives 32/a = −8, so a = −4. That is the only value that works, so it is also the greatest possible value.

Rewrite as 4x^2 − 32x + (19 − r) = 0. A quadratic has exactly one real solution when its discriminant is 0: (−32)^2 − 4(4)(19 − r) = 0, so 1,024 = 16(19 − r) and 19 − r = 64. Therefore r = −45.

All four forms equal 48(64)^x. Increasing x by 2 multiplies f by 64^2 = 4,096, so c = 4,096. Choice D, f(x) = 48(4,096)^(x/2), shows c as the base: each increase of 2 in x adds 1 to the exponent x/2. Choice C shows 64, which is the factor for an increase of 1, not 2.
